notes.text: I'm going to start by calling the get_mission tool.

I'm laying out the plan: six unknowns to pin down. I'm thinking test drops at different altitudes can measure wind at altitude and fall time, with drops near the fire center to spot updrafts through the smoke flag.

I'm working out how the wind changes with altitude: test drops at about 30 m and 150 m should show the shear and veer. Fall time from 100 m is roughly 4.5 s without drag, and drag only nudges that, mainly by pulling the load's horizontal velocity toward the wind. For the first test drop I'm looking at a release outside the smoke, past the 50 m calibration radius, and I'm debating whether to drop near the center at all, since an updraft there would skew the fall time.

I'm pulling the wind readings at three heights: 10.7 m/s at 100 m, 8.1 m/s at 30 m, and 11.3 m/s at 150 m. To fit a power-law shear exponent, I'm taking the ratio 8.1/10.7 ≈ 0.757 and solving (0.3)^s = 0.757, which gives s ≈ 0.23. Next I'll check that exponent against the 150 m reading.

Now I'm estimating the shear exponent from the 150 m reading, which gives about 0.13, so the average with the 100 m fit lands near 0.18. Next I'm checking the wind direction at each height, which turns about 5 degrees per 50 m, and the rough veer I get from it is noisy.

I'm now working through the terminal-velocity model for the fall, using quadratic drag with the speed profile tied to tanh and the distance tied to a log-cosh term. Taking the drag constant as 0.03, I'm checking whether the predicted fall from 100 m matches the 7.19 s measured time.

Now I'm checking the drag constant against the 100 m drop: k around 0.033 overshoots, and 0.035 undershoots the height, so it settles near 0.0355.

Checking the drag estimate at h=30 m against the 3.24 s fall, my current constant of 0.0355 gives roughly 35 m instead of 30, so something doesn't line up. I'm now testing a much larger drag constant, around 0.08, to see whether it brings the predicted distance down to the measured height.

Now I'm testing the drag constant against the 30 m drop, where the fall time gives about 0.06, which doesn't match the 0.0355 from the 100 m drop. The mismatch makes me suspect the horizontal relative velocity also feeds into the drag, since the aircraft's 60 m/s minus the wind changes the total relative speed.

I'm realizing the horizontal relative velocity matters here: the aircraft's 60 m/s against the wind adds a large sideways component, so drag couples the horizontal and vertical motion. That means the vertical fall can't be solved on its own and would need a simulation. Next I want drops that pin down the drag, since its size drives how the fall goes.

I'm going to test a hypothesis for the drag, wind, and shear: drag 0.035, wind 10.7 m/s from 206°, shear 0.18, veer -6, no updraft. Then I'll compare the predicted drops against the measured ones to see where the residuals fall.

I'm checking the drag values against the dt errors, where a higher drag gives a larger positive error at 0.06, which points toward lowering the drag.

I'm working out whether lowering the drag actually shortens the predicted fall time, since going from 0.06 to 0.035 cut the test-one error from 1.97 down to 0.47. That would mean the model is too slow, so I'm estimating how much further the drag needs to drop to close the remaining gap.
